title: Do You Even Know What Youre Defending
author: Dempsey, Patrick
summary: Patrick Dempsey traces the intellectual and political history of the modern education system to argue that defenders of its core structures are unwittingly defending a system designed not for human flourishing but for state obedience, industrial efficiency, and cognitive reduction. Through a chronological tour -- Descartes' cogito (1641), Adam Smith's factory pin division (1776), Napoleon's Prussian military-obedience school model (1806), Horace Mann's Prussian import to Boston (1837), the Committee of Ten's university-admission-driven curriculum standardisation (1892), and Frederick Taylor's scientific management (1911) -- Dempsey builds the case that modern schooling's shape was determined by forces hostile to holistic human formation. The piece's rhetorical strategy is to reframe the debate: critics of the system are not 'anti-education' or 'pro-AI-shill'; they are asking whether the artefacts of the system (essays, exams, rigor, discrete subjects, grade-level sequencing) serve human flourishing or serve the institutional logics that built them. Dempsey argues that defenders who assume the system uniquely benefits human flourishing have not examined the historical record of what the system was actually designed to do -- and that AI's emergence is simply exposing that confusion more rapidly and visibly.
points: The modern education system's core design decisions were made not to optimise for human flourishing but to serve specific historical forces: Prussian military obedience, industrial pin-factory efficiency, university admission requirements, and Taylorist scientific management.

Descartes' 'I think, therefore I am' established cognition as the defining feature of humanness, which Western institutions -- including schools -- subsequently optimised around, to the exclusion of embodied, relational, spiritual, and aesthetic dimensions of persons.

Adam Smith's factory division-of-labour logic was absorbed directly into the school model 50 years after The Wealth of Nations: discrete subjects taught sequentially represent the fragmentation of human knowledge into industrially manageable specialised steps.

Napoleon's generals, having lost to a better-drilled army, designed compulsory schooling to produce citizens who follow orders without asking why -- a military project whose obedience-formation logic is still embedded in the structures (bells, compliance, standardised response) defenders of the system are defending.

The loudest defenders of school artefacts (essays, exams, rigor, ritual) are often the same people who believe the system uniquely benefits human flourishing -- but have not examined whether those artefacts were designed with human flourishing as their purpose.
quotes: The things they're defending -- the essays, the exams, the rigor, the ritual, and all the other artifacts of the system they deem as possibly imperfect, but by no means broken -- are products of a system designed specifically contrary to human flourishing.

1641 -- Rene Descartes, Netherlands. Sitting alone in a heated room by candlelight, he decides the mind and body are fundamentally separate substances. I think, therefore I am. Not, I have a family, therefore I am. Not I love my dog, therefore I am.

Adam Smith visits a pin factory -- the needle for industrial sewing machines -- and sees the average person make 20 pins. Then he visits another factory and watches workers produce 48,000 pins a day by dividing the job into eighteen specialized steps. He goes home and writes The Wealth of Nations. Fragment any human activity into its smallest parts and optimize each one. Schools will absorb this logic fifty years later.

Prussian generals are sitting by candlelight trying to understand how Napoleon destroyed their entire army in a single afternoon. Their conclusion: our soldiers ran because they lacked obedience and loyalty to the state. Their solution: build compulsory schools. The factory model of education is born as a military project.

Ten university presidents, chaired by Harvard's president, convene to decide what every American child should learn -- based on what universities want for admissions. They fragment human knowledge into siloed subjects divided by bells. The academic hierarchy that still governs schools today is decided in a single meeting.

Cognition as what it means to be human. Everything that happens after this, intentionally or otherwise, takes this idea as its lead. And the consequence is that everything we do in Western culture is designed to maximize the efficiency by which information gets put into the brain.
